AWS Object Storage and AWS S3 Bucket

Store, protect, secure, and optimize objects in Amazon S3 with buckets, storage classes, lifecycle rules, versioning, replication, access control, encryption, and cost controls.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

AWS Storage Services

AWS offers storage services for block, file, and object data, plus hybrid storage and data transfer, and backup. This lesson covers object storage, which is Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).

This lesson explains how Amazon S3 stores data as objects in buckets, and how to choose and configure it. It covers buckets and objects, storage classes, lifecycle rules, versioning, Object Lock, replication, access control, encryption, performance, hosting and event features, and pricing. Hybrid storage with AWS Storage Gateway is covered in Lesson 271.3. The last three tabs bring the parts together for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam.

The tabs in this lesson cover the following topics:

  • Tab 1: object storage, how it differs from block and file storage, and the core facts about Amazon S3.
  • Tab 2: buckets, objects, keys, prefixes, addressing, and uploads.
  • Tab 3: the S3 storage classes and how to choose one.
  • Tab 4: lifecycle rules and S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
  • Tab 5: versioning, delete markers, MFA Delete, and S3 Object Lock.
  • Tab 6: Cross-Region Replication, Same-Region Replication, and Replication Time Control.
  • Tab 7: IAM policies, bucket policies, Block Public Access, presigned URLs, access points, and VPC endpoints.
  • Tab 8: encryption in transit and at rest, and the server-side and client-side options.
  • Tab 9: request rates, multipart upload, byte-range fetches, and Transfer Acceleration.
  • Tab 10: static website hosting, CORS, and event notifications.
  • Tab 11: server access logs, Requester Pays, S3 Inventory, S3 Batch Operations, and S3 Storage Lens.
  • Tab 12: Amazon Macie, which discovers and protects sensitive data in Amazon S3.
  • Tab 13: what Amazon S3 charges for, worked cost examples, and ways to lower the cost.
  • Tab 14: a practice assignment on AWS Skill Builder.
  • Tab 15: comparison tables and the SAA-C03 cheat sheet with decision rules.

Introduction

Almost every AWS architecture stores files: images, backups, logs, reports, and data for analytics. Amazon S3 is the service that holds most of them. It never asks you to size a disk, it keeps data durable across multiple data centers, and it offers several storage classes that cost less as data ages. Architects who pass SAA-C03 questions on storage, security, and cost need to know which S3 feature solves which problem.

This lesson assumes basic AWS knowledge, such as using the console and recognizing Regions and Availability Zones. It follows FlashCart Inc., an online store, through the Problem Statement of each tab.

Use the tab list on the left, or the Previous and Next buttons, to move through the lesson. Each topic tab opens with a Problem Statement and ends with exam traps, keyword triggers, and resource links. The Knowledge Check is the last tab.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

  1. Define object storage, bucket, object, key, and prefix.
  2. Explain how Amazon S3 provides durability, availability, and strong consistency.
  3. Compare Amazon S3 with block storage and file storage.
  4. Select the S3 storage class that fits a stated access pattern, retrieval time, and cost.
  5. Apply lifecycle rules and S3 Intelligent-Tiering to move or expire objects.
  6. Describe versioning, delete markers, and S3 Object Lock for data protection.
  7. Describe replication and when it meets resilience and compliance requirements.
  8. Evaluate the S3 access control options, and choose among the encryption options.
  9. Explain how Amazon Macie discovers and reports sensitive data in Amazon S3.
  10. Recommend performance, hosting, and cost-optimization approaches for a stated workload.
  11. Design a secure, resilient, and cost-aware S3 architecture for a stated workload.

Two terms appear often in this lesson:

  • Durability: the likelihood that data is not lost. Availability: the likelihood that data can be reached when you ask for it.
  • Prefix: the leading part of an object key, such as images/2026/, that groups objects.

1. Object Storage and Amazon S3 Basics

Problem Statement

FlashCart Inc., an online store, keeps product photos, customer invoices, and clickstream logs. The files must be reachable over HTTPS, must survive the loss of a data center, must grow without anyone planning disk sizes, and must cost less as they age. The team needs to know what kind of storage fits this job and what Amazon S3 offers.

1.1 What Object Storage Is

Object storage works as follows:

  • Object storage keeps data as objects. Each object holds the data itself, metadata that describes it, and a unique identifier called a key.
  • The namespace is flat. There is no tree of folders and no disk to mount. You address an object by its key.
  • You reach objects through an HTTP or HTTPS Application Programming Interface (API), not through a file system or a block device.
  • An object is written and read as a whole. To change an object, you upload a new version of it. You do not edit a few bytes in place.
  • Object storage scales to very large numbers of objects and suits unstructured data such as images, video, backups, logs, and data lake files.

1.2 Block, File, and Object Storage

QuestionBlock storageFile storageObject storage
AWS servicesAmazon EBS and instance store.Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx.Amazon S3.
How it is accessedAttached to an instance as a drive.Mounted as a shared network file system.Through an HTTP or HTTPS API, by bucket and key.
StructureFixed-size blocks on a volume.Files in folders.Flat set of objects in buckets.
Change a small part of the dataYes, in place.Yes, in place.No. Upload the whole object again.
Best forOperating systems, databases, boot volumes.Shared files for many servers.Backups, media, logs, data lakes, static content, and archives.

1.3 What Amazon S3 Is

Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is an object storage service. It stores data as objects inside containers called buckets.

Amazon S3 has these core characteristics:

  • Amazon S3 is the object storage service of AWS. You store objects in buckets, and you pay for the storage you use.
  • Capacity is virtually unlimited. You never provision a size.
  • Every S3 storage class is designed for 99.999999999 percent durability, often called eleven nines.
  • S3 Standard is designed for 99.99 percent availability.
  • Most storage classes store data redundantly in at least three Availability Zones of a Region. The One Zone classes store data in one zone.
  • A bucket belongs to one Region. Your data stays in that Region unless you copy or replicate it.
  • You use S3 through the AWS Management Console, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and the REST API.
  • Amazon S3 is one of the main building blocks of AWS. Many websites use it as a backbone, and many AWS services use it to integrate with each other.
  • S3 looks like a global service, but you create each bucket in one Region.
  • Durability example: if you store 10,000,000 objects in Amazon S3, you can on average expect to lose a single object once every 10,000 years.
  • Availability example: 99.99 percent availability means that the service is unavailable for about 53 minutes in a year.

1.3.1 How Does S3 Work?

S3 uses a simple structure: Bucket → Object → Data.

  • Bucket: the container that holds your objects.
    • Bucket example: my-website-images
  • Object: an item in a bucket, identified by its key, with its data and its metadata.
    • For example:
      • profile.jpg
      • resume.pdf
      • video.mp4
      • logo.png
  • Data: the content of the object that you upload and read.

1.4 Strong Consistency

  • Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all object operations.
  • After a successful write of a new object, or an overwrite or delete of an existing object, any later read returns the latest data.
  • List operations also reflect the latest changes.
  • Strong consistency adds no extra cost and does not reduce performance.

1.5 Size Limits

LimitValue
Maximum size of one object50 TB. Amazon S3 raised this from 5 TB in December 2025.
Maximum size of one upload in a single PUT request5 GB.
Upload method for objects larger than 5 GBMultipart upload.
Recommended upload method for objects larger than 100 MBMultipart upload.

Older SAA-C03 study material says that the maximum object size is 5 TB. Learn the current value, and read exam questions carefully.

1.6 Common Use Cases

  • Backups, disaster recovery copies, and archives.
  • Hybrid cloud storage.
  • Application hosting and media hosting.
  • Data lakes and big data analytics.
  • Images, video, and other media for web and mobile applications.
  • Static website content.
  • Log storage, including long-term compliance archives.
  • Software delivery and application data.

Examples from industry: Nasdaq stores seven years of data in S3 Glacier, and Sysco runs analytics on its data in S3 to gain business insights.

1.7 Advanced S3 Features

S3 includes several features for managing large amounts of data:

  • Multipart Upload: upload large files in smaller parts, often in parallel.
  • S3 Batch Operations: perform actions such as copying, tagging, or deleting many objects at once.
  • Replication: automatically copy objects to another bucket in the same or a different AWS Region.
  • Event Notifications: trigger services such as AWS Lambda, SQS, or SNS when objects are created or deleted.

1.8 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

AWS provides tools such as CloudWatch and CloudTrail to monitor activity and troubleshoot problems.

Common S3 issues include access denied errors, incorrect bucket policies, missing buckets, and permission problems. Checking IAM roles, bucket policies, encryption settings, and logs can help identify these issues.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A web application lets users upload images. The images must be durable and reachable over HTTPS. The number of images is unpredictable, and the team does not want to plan disk capacity. Which storage should the architect choose?

  • A. An EBS volume attached to the web server.
  • B. An instance store volume on the web server.
  • C. An Amazon S3 bucket.
  • D. An Amazon EFS file system mounted on the web server.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. Amazon S3 stores unstructured objects with eleven nines of durability, scales without capacity planning, and serves objects over HTTPS.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectAn EBS volume has a provisioned size, lives in one Availability Zone, and is not served over HTTPS by itself.
BIncorrectInstance store is temporary and is lost when the instance stops.
CCorrectS3 is durable, scales without planning, and serves objects over HTTPS.
DIncorrectEFS provides a shared file system for servers, and it is not the best fit for web-served objects.

Exam Trap

Amazon S3 is not a file system. A question that needs a drive an instance can mount, or a file system shared by many instances, does not point to S3. It points to Amazon EBS or Amazon EFS. S3 holds objects that you reach through an API.

Memory Hook

S3 = objects in buckets, found by key, over HTTP.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Virtually unlimited, durable storage for unstructured data"
→ Amazon S3

Trigger 2: "Eleven nines of durability"
→ Amazon S3, in any storage class

Trigger 3: "Store static assets, backups, or a data lake"
→ Amazon S3

Trigger 4: "A shared POSIX file system for many Linux instances"
→ Amazon EFS, not Amazon S3

Trigger 5: "A boot or database drive for one instance"
→ Amazon EBS, not Amazon S3

2. Buckets and Objects

Problem Statement

Two FlashCart teams try to create a bucket with the same name, and one of them is surprised that the name is already taken. A developer wants to rename a bucket and to create folders in it. Another developer uploads an 8 GB product video, and the single upload fails. The team needs to understand how buckets, objects, keys, and uploads work.

2.1 Buckets

A bucket is the container for objects. Buckets work as follows:

  • A bucket name must be unique within its namespace. The traditional model is a globally unique name (section 2.2.1).
  • A bucket name follows these rules:
    • It has 3 to 63 characters.
    • It uses lowercase letters, numbers, dots, and hyphens.
    • It begins and ends with a letter or a number.
    • It must not start with the prefix xn--.
    • It must not end with the suffix -s3alias.
  • A bucket name must not look like an IP address.
  • A bucket name cannot contain uppercase letters or underscores.
  • You choose the Region when you create the bucket. You cannot move a bucket to another Region.
  • You cannot rename a bucket. To use another name, create a new bucket, copy the objects, and delete the old bucket.
  • The bucket Amazon Resource Name (ARN) has the form arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name.
  • An account has a quota on the number of buckets. Check the AWS service quotas for the current limit.
  • S3 offers several bucket types. The most common is the general purpose bucket (section 2.2).

2.2 Bucket Types

Amazon S3 offers four bucket types: general purpose buckets, directory buckets, table buckets, and vector buckets.

2.2.1 General Purpose Buckets

Use general purpose buckets for:

  • Application data.
  • Backups.
  • Logs.
  • Static website files.
  • Media.
  • Data lakes.
  • Archived records.
  • CloudFront origins.
  • Analytics datasets.

General purpose buckets support most S3 features and storage classes.

Bucket Namespace

General purpose buckets can currently be created in:

  • Shared global namespace: the name must be unique across AWS accounts and Regions within an AWS partition.
  • Account regional namespace: the name is reserved for a specific account and Region.

The account regional namespace is a newer capability. For SAA-C03 preparation, learners should still recognize globally unique bucket names as the traditional and commonly tested model.

2.2.2 Directory Buckets

Directory buckets:

  • Use S3 Express One Zone.
  • Store data in one Availability Zone.
  • Organize data hierarchically.
  • Provide very low-latency access.
  • Support latency-sensitive applications.
  • Do not support every general purpose bucket feature.

2.2.3 Table Buckets

Table buckets store tables in the Apache Iceberg format. They integrate with services such as Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, AWS Glue, and Apache Spark.

2.2.4 Vector Buckets

Vector buckets are designed for vector storage and similarity searches. A vector bucket contains one or more vector indexes, and it can support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications.

2.3 Bucket Identity and Configuration

2.3.1 Bucket Identity

An S3 bucket is defined by:

  • Bucket name.
  • Bucket type.
  • AWS Region.
  • AWS account owner.
  • Creation date.
  • Amazon Resource Name (ARN).
  • Namespace type.

Important characteristics:

  • A bucket is created in an AWS Region.
  • General purpose bucket data is normally stored redundantly across multiple Availability Zones.
  • A bucket cannot be moved directly to another Region.
  • Objects can be copied or replicated to a bucket in another Region.
  • Bucket names should not contain sensitive information, because they may appear in URLs and logs.
  • Deleting a bucket does not automatically transfer its name or contents elsewhere.

The settings of a bucket fall into six groups:

2.4 Objects

Each object consists of these parts:

PartWhat it isNotes
KeyThe unique name of the object in the bucket.Up to 1,024 bytes of UTF-8 text.
ValueThe data of the object.Up to 50 TB.
Version IDAn identifier of one version of the object.Present when versioning is enabled.
System metadataInformation such as content type, size, and last modified date.Set by S3 or by the upload request.
User-defined metadataName and value pairs that you add.Sent with the header prefix x-amz-meta-.
TagsKey and value pairs for classification, access control, and lifecycle rules.Up to 10 tags per object. Tags help with security and lifecycle rules.
Storage classThe class that stores the object.Set at upload or changed later.
  • Object values are the content of the body:
    • The maximum object size is 50 TB (50,000 GB).
    • If you upload more than 5 GB, you must use multipart upload.

2.4.1 Object User-Defined Metadata vs. Tags

  • User-defined metadata
    • It consists of key and value pairs stored inside the metadata of the object.
    • You add it only at the time of upload, with a PUT or POST request.
    • You cannot modify it later without re-uploading the object.
    • The keys are stored as HTTP headers and sent back on every GET request.
    • Applications mostly use it to store custom information.
    • Examples:
      • x-amz-meta-source: camera-1
      • x-amz-meta-resolution: 1080p
  • Tags
    • They are key and value pairs stored separately from the metadata of the object.
    • You can add, update, or remove them at any time.
    • They are not returned with the object payload. You use a separate API to read them.
    • AWS services use them for automation and governance:
      • Lifecycle transitions.
      • Expiration.
      • Replication.
      • Object Lock retention rules.
      • Access controls (IAM conditions).
      • S3 Inventory filtering.
    • Examples:
      • env=development
      • tier=premium
  • How to choose
    • Use metadata for custom information that travels with the object and that an application reads.
    • Use tags for information that policies, lifecycle rules, and other AWS services use to manage the object.

2.5 Keys and Prefixes

  • The key is the full path of the object:
    • s3://my-bucket/my_file.txt
    • s3://my-bucket/my_folder1/another_folder/my_file.txt
  • The key is composed of a prefix plus the object name:
    • s3://my-bucket/my_folder1/another_folder/my_file.txt
    • The prefix is my_folder1/another_folder/, and the object name is my_file.txt.
  • There is no concept of directories within buckets, although the console user interface can make it look as if there is:
    • The S3 namespace is flat.
    • A key is just a very long name that contains slashes.
    • A delimiter, usually a slash, separates the parts of a key. The key images/2026/logo.png has the prefix images/2026/.
  • Prefixes matter for performance, because request rates apply to each prefix (tab 9), and for permissions and lifecycle rules, which can target a prefix.
  • You cannot rename an object. To change its key, copy the object to the new key and delete the old one.

2.6 Addressing an Object

StyleExampleNotes
Virtual-hosted stylehttps://flowcart-media.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/images/2026/logo.pngThe bucket name is part of the host name. This style is recommended.

2.7 Uploading and Copying Objects

  • A single PUT request uploads an object of up to 5 GB.
  • Use multipart upload for large objects. It is required above 5 GB and recommended above 100 MB.
  • Multipart upload splits an object into parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB (the last part can be smaller), with up to 10,000 parts. The parts upload in parallel, and S3 assembles the object.
  • If one part fails, you retry only that part, not the whole object.
  • An unfinished multipart upload keeps its parts and bills for them. Add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads (tab 4).
  • You can upload with the console, the AWS CLI (for example aws s3 cp and aws s3 sync), the AWS SDKs, or a presigned URL.
  • A copy operation copies an object within S3. Objects larger than 5 GB need a multipart copy.

2.8 Deleting Buckets and Objects

  • A bucket must be empty before you delete it.
  • In a bucket with versioning, you must delete all versions and delete markers first (tab 5).
  • Deleting an object removes it from the bucket, and in a versioned bucket it adds a delete marker.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A developer uploads an 8 GB video to Amazon S3 with a single PUT request, and the upload fails. The developer wants a fast, reliable upload that retries only the parts that fail. What should the developer use?

  • A. Compress the video and retry the single PUT request.
  • B. Use a multipart upload.
  • C. Upload the video to an EBS volume and attach it to S3.
  • D. Rename the bucket to use a shorter name.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: B. A single PUT request supports at most 5 GB. Multipart upload splits the object into parts that upload in parallel, and S3 retries only a failed part.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA single PUT request supports at most 5 GB, so this approach is unreliable for an 8 GB file.
BCorrectMultipart upload is required above 5 GB, and it retries only the failed parts.
CIncorrectAn EBS volume is block storage. It cannot be attached to S3.
DIncorrectThe bucket name does not affect the upload size limit.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • Bucket names are globally unique, and a bucket cannot be renamed or moved to another Region.
  • S3 has no real folders. A prefix is part of the key.
  • Objects above 5 GB need multipart upload.

Memory Hook

Bucket = global name, one Region. Key = prefix + name. Over 5 GB = multipart.

3. S3 Storage Classes

Problem Statement

FlashCart stores product photos that customers view every day, invoices that auditors open about once a quarter, and seven years of tax records that nobody opens unless there is an audit. All of it sits in S3 Standard, and the bill is high. The team must choose a storage class for each kind of data and understand the retrieval times and the minimum charges.

3.1 What a Storage Class Is

  • A storage class sets how S3 stores an object, and with it the price, the availability, the retrieval time, and the retrieval charges.
  • You choose the class when you upload an object, or you change it later with a lifecycle rule or a copy.
  • All classes are designed for eleven nines of durability. They differ in availability, the number of Availability Zones, retrieval, and cost.
  • As a rule, the cheaper the storage is per GB, the higher the retrieval charge or the slower the retrieval.

3.2 Class Details

3.2.1 S3 Standard

  • The default class. It is designed for 99.99 percent availability and stores data in at least three Availability Zones.
  • It gives low latency and high throughput, and it can sustain two concurrent facility failures.
  • Use it for frequently accessed data, such as big data analytics, mobile and gaming applications, website content, and content distribution.

3.2.2 S3 Intelligent-Tiering

  • It moves objects between access tiers automatically based on how often you use them (tab 4).
  • It has no retrieval fees. It charges a small monitoring and automation fee per 1,000 objects.
  • Use it when you cannot predict the access pattern.

3.2.3 S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA

  • Both are for data you read rarely but need in milliseconds. They charge a retrieval fee for each GB retrieved.
  • Standard-IA stores data in at least three Availability Zones and is designed for 99.9 percent availability. Use it for disaster recovery copies and backups.
  • One Zone-IA stores data in one Availability Zone, is designed for 99.5 percent availability, and costs less. If that zone is destroyed, the data is lost, so use it only for data that you can recreate, such as secondary backup copies of on-premises data.
  • Both have a 30-day minimum storage duration and a 128 KB minimum billable object size.

3.2.4 The S3 Glacier Classes

  • Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access to archive data, and it suits data that you access about once a quarter. It has a 90-day minimum duration and a 128 KB minimum billable object size.
  • Glacier Flexible Retrieval is for archives that can wait. You request a restore first, which creates a temporary copy that you can read. It offers Expedited, Standard, and Bulk retrieval, and Bulk retrieval is free. It has a 90-day minimum duration.
  • Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class, for data you access rarely or once or twice a year. It offers Standard and Bulk retrieval, and it has a 180-day minimum duration.

3.2.5 S3 Express One Zone

  • It is a high-performance storage class that stores objects in a directory bucket, which is a bucket in a single Availability Zone that you choose.
  • It handles hundreds of thousands of requests per second with single-digit millisecond latency, and the course slides state up to 10 times better performance than S3 Standard.
  • It is designed for 99.999999999 percent durability and 99.95 percent availability.
  • Place your storage and compute in the same Availability Zone to reduce latency. A directory bucket name includes the zone ID, for example stephane--use1-az4--x-s3.
  • It costs more per GB than S3 Standard. Use it for latency-sensitive and data-intensive applications such as machine learning training, financial modeling, media processing, and high performance computing.
  • It integrates well with Amazon SageMaker Model Training, Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue.

S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval99.9 percent99 percent128 KB
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval99.99 percent99.9 percent40 KB
S3 Glacier Deep Archive99.99 percent99.9 percent40 KB
S3 Express One Zone99.95 percentNot listed in the course slidesNot listed in the course slides

3.4 Minimum Charges

  • Minimum storage duration: if you delete or move an object before the minimum duration ends, you are charged for the remaining days. The minimums are 30 days for the IA classes, 90 days for Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval, and 180 days for Deep Archive.
  • Minimum billable object size: the IA classes and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill at least 128 KB for each object, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive bill at least 40 KB, even if the object is smaller. Storing millions of tiny objects in these classes costs more than expected.

3.5 Choosing a Storage Class

If the data is...Choose
Accessed often.S3 Standard.
Accessed in an unpredictable way.S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
Accessed rarely, and needed in milliseconds, in several zones.S3 Standard-IA.
Accessed rarely, needed in milliseconds, and easy to recreate.S3 One Zone-IA.
Archive data that is rarely read but must be available at once.S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
Archive data where a wait of minutes or hours is acceptable.S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
Long-term archive that is almost never read.S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Needed with the lowest possible latency.S3 Express One Zone.

3.5.1 Storage-Class Decision Flow

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company must keep seven years of financial records for audits. The records are almost never read, and a retrieval time of up to 12 hours is acceptable. The company wants the lowest storage cost. Which storage class meets the requirement?

  • A. S3 Standard.
  • B. S3 Standard-IA.
  • C. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
  • D. S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class, and its Standard retrieval completes within 12 hours.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectS3 Standard has the highest storage cost for data that is almost never read.
BIncorrectStandard-IA costs more than the archive classes and adds retrieval fees.
CIncorrectGlacier Instant Retrieval gives immediate access that the requirement does not need, at a higher price.
DCorrectDeep Archive has the lowest cost and meets the 12-hour retrieval window.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • One Zone-IA keeps data in one Availability Zone. It is not for data that you cannot recreate.
  • Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive need a restore before you can read an object. Glacier Instant Retrieval does not.
  • Early deletion and tiny objects trigger minimum charges in the IA and Glacier classes.

Memory Hook

Standard = hot. IA = cool, fast. Glacier = archive. Deep Archive = frozen. One Zone = one zone only.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Infrequent access, rapid retrieval, data can be recreated"
→ S3 One Zone-IA

Trigger 2: "Unknown or changing access patterns, no retrieval fees"
→ S3 Intelligent-Tiering

Trigger 3: "Archive with millisecond retrieval"
→ S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval

Trigger 4: "Archive, retrieval in minutes to hours"
→ S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval

Trigger 5: "Cheapest storage, retrieval within 12 or 48 hours"
→ S3 Glacier Deep Archive

Useful Resources

  • Docs Amazon S3 storage classes
  • Pricing Amazon S3 pricing

4. Lifecycle and Intelligent-Tiering

Problem Statement

FlashCart keeps application logs. The team reads the logs every day for the first month, rarely for the next two months, and almost never after that. The logs must be kept for seven years and then deleted. Nobody wants to move the files by hand, and some bucket data is accessed in a pattern that nobody can predict. The team needs rules that move and delete data automatically.

4.1 S3 Lifecycle Rules

A lifecycle configuration is a set of rules that S3 applies to objects automatically:

  • A transition action moves objects to another storage class after a number of days.
  • An expiration action deletes objects after a number of days.
  • A rule can apply to the whole bucket, to a prefix, to objects with certain tags, or to objects of a certain size.
  • In a versioned bucket, separate rules handle the current version and the noncurrent versions of objects.
  • A rule can remove expired delete markers, and a rule can abort incomplete multipart uploads after a number of days.

4.2 Transition Rules

  • Objects move down the classes: from Standard to Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and Glacier Deep Archive. A lifecycle rule cannot move an object back up to a warmer class.
  • Objects must stay in S3 Standard for at least 30 days before a rule moves them to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA.
  • Each class has its own minimum storage duration, so moving objects too early can cost more (tab 3).
  • Very small objects cost more in the IA classes because of the 128 KB minimum billable size. A rule can use an object size filter to leave them in Standard.
  • Use S3 Storage Class Analysis or the access data in S3 Storage Lens to see when data becomes infrequently accessed.

4.3 Expiration Rules

  • An expiration rule deletes the current version of an object. In a bucket with versioning it adds a delete marker instead.
  • A noncurrent version expiration rule permanently deletes old versions after a number of days, which controls the cost of versioning.
  • Lifecycle rules run asynchronously. An object can remain for a short time after it expires.

4.4 S3 Intelligent-Tiering

S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between tiers automatically, based on its own access pattern:

TierWhen an object moves thereAccess to the object
Frequent AccessWhen the object is first stored and whenever it is accessed.Milliseconds.
Infrequent AccessAfter 30 days without access.Milliseconds.
Archive Instant AccessAfter 90 days without access.Milliseconds.
Archive Access (optional)After a period without access that you configure, from 90 days.Minutes to hours. You restore the object.
Deep Archive Access (optional)After a period without access that you configure, from 180 days.Hours. You restore the object.
  • There are no retrieval fees, and moving objects between tiers has no extra charge. S3 charges a small monitoring and automation fee per 1,000 objects.
  • Objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored, so they stay in the Frequent Access tier.
  • An object that you access again returns to the Frequent Access tier.
  • Use Intelligent-Tiering when the access pattern is unknown or changes. Use a lifecycle rule when the pattern is predictable.

4.5 Lifecycle Rules and Intelligent-Tiering Compared

QuestionLifecycle ruleS3 Intelligent-Tiering
Who decides when an object moves?You, by age in days.S3, by the access pattern of each object.
Best when the access pattern is...Predictable, such as logs that cool with age.Unknown or changing.
Can delete objects?Yes, with an expiration rule.No. Combine it with a lifecycle rule.
Retrieval fees?Yes, in IA and Glacier classes.None.
Extra fee?Per-request transition fee.Monitoring and automation fee per 1,000 objects.

4.6 Lifecycle Rule Examples

  • Transition: move objects to S3 Standard-IA 60 days after creation, and move them to Glacier for archiving after six months.
  • Expiration: delete access log files after 365 days.
  • Versions: delete old versions of files when versioning is enabled.
  • Multipart uploads: delete incomplete multipart uploads.
  • Scope by prefix: apply a rule only to the objects under a prefix, for example s3://mybucket/mp3/*.
  • Scope by tag: apply a rule only to the objects with a tag, for example Department: Finance.

4.7 Lifecycle Scenarios

4.7.1 Scenario 1: Profile Photos and Thumbnails

An application on EC2 creates thumbnails after profile photos are uploaded to Amazon S3. The thumbnails are easy to recreate and need to be kept for only 60 days. The source images must be retrievable immediately for 60 days, and afterwards the user can wait up to six hours.

  • Keep the source images in S3 Standard, and add a lifecycle rule that transitions them to Glacier after 60 days. A wait of up to six hours fits Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
  • Keep the thumbnails in S3 One Zone-IA, because they can be recreated, and add a lifecycle rule that expires them after 60 days.

4.7.2 Scenario 2: Recovering Deleted Objects

A company rule says that deleted S3 objects must be recoverable immediately for 30 days, although this happens rarely. After that, and for up to 365 days, deleted objects must be recoverable within 48 hours.

  • Enable S3 Versioning, so that a deleted object is only hidden by a delete marker and can be recovered.
  • Transition the noncurrent versions of the object to S3 Standard-IA.
  • Later, transition the noncurrent versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which restores within 48 hours.

4.8 S3 Storage Class Analysis

  • S3 Storage Class Analysis helps you decide when to transition objects to the right storage class.
  • It gives recommendations for S3 Standard and S3 Standard-IA. It does not work for S3 One Zone-IA or the Glacier classes.
  • The report updates daily, and it takes 24 to 48 hours before you see the first data.
  • The report is a CSV file that shows the date, the storage class, and the object age.
  • It is a good first step when you put together lifecycle rules or improve them.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company stores logs in S3. The company reads them often for 30 days and then rarely. The logs must be deleted after seven years, and the company wants no manual work. Which solution meets the requirement at the lowest cost?

  • A. Create a lifecycle rule that moves the logs to a colder class after 30 days and expires them after seven years.
  • B. Keep the logs in S3 Standard and delete them by hand after seven years.
  • C. Move the logs to an EBS volume after 30 days.
  • D. Enable replication of the logs to another Region.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. A lifecycle rule automates both the transition to a colder class and the expiration, which lowers the cost and removes manual work.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectA lifecycle rule handles transitions and expiration automatically.
BIncorrectS3 Standard costs more than a colder class for rarely read data, and manual deletion is manual work.
CIncorrectEBS is block storage and does not suit log archives.
DIncorrectReplication copies data and adds cost. It does not move or delete logs.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • Lifecycle rules move objects down only, and objects stay 30 days in Standard before a move to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA.
  • Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval fees but has a per-object monitoring fee, and it does not delete objects.
  • Add a rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads, or the leftover parts keep billing.

Memory Hook

Predictable = lifecycle. Unpredictable = Intelligent-Tiering. Clean up uploads and old versions.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Move objects to a cheaper class automatically after 30 days"
→ Lifecycle transition rule

Trigger 2: "Delete objects automatically after a period"
→ Lifecycle expiration rule

Trigger 3: "Unpredictable access pattern, no retrieval fees"
→ S3 Intelligent-Tiering

Trigger 4: "Control the cost of old object versions"
→ Noncurrent version expiration rule

5. Versioning and Object Lock

Problem Statement

A FlashCart engineer overwrites a product price file by mistake, and another engineer deletes a folder of invoices. The team cannot recover either one. The auditors also require that certain financial records can never be changed or deleted for seven years, even by an administrator. The team needs ways to recover from mistakes and to lock data.

5.1 Versioning

Versioning keeps every version of every object in a bucket:

  • A bucket is unversioned by default. You can enable versioning, and later you can suspend it. You cannot return a bucket to the unversioned state.
  • With versioning enabled, S3 gives every object a unique version ID. An overwrite creates a new version and keeps the old one.
  • Versioning is enabled at the bucket level, and it is a best practice to version your buckets.
  • Versioning protects against accidental overwrites and deletes, and it lets you restore an earlier version.
  • Every version bills for storage, so combine versioning with a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions.
  • Objects that existed before you enabled versioning get the version ID null.
  • Suspending versioning does not delete the previous versions.

5.2 Delete Markers

  • A normal delete in a versioned bucket does not remove any data. S3 adds a delete marker, and the object seems to be gone: a GET request returns a 404 error.
  • To restore the object, delete the delete marker.
  • To delete a version permanently, delete it by its version ID.

5.3 MFA Delete

  • With multi-factor authentication (MFA), users must generate a code on a device, such as a mobile phone or a hardware device, before an important operation.
  • MFA is required to permanently delete an object version and to suspend versioning on the bucket.
  • MFA is not required to enable versioning or to list deleted versions.
  • To use MFA Delete, versioning must be enabled on the bucket, and only the bucket owner (the root account) can enable or disable MFA Delete.

5.4 S3 Object Lock

S3 Object Lock stores objects with a write once, read many (WORM) model, so that an object version cannot be overwritten or deleted for a fixed time:

  • Object Lock needs versioning, and it protects individual object versions.
  • A retention period locks a version for a number of days or years, or until a date.
  • A legal hold locks a version until someone removes the hold. It has no expiry date and works independently of a retention period.
  • You can extend a retention period. You place and remove a legal hold with the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission.
  • You can set a default retention for a bucket, so that new objects are locked automatically.
Retention modeWho can override itUse it for
Governance modeUsers with a special permission can change or remove the lock and delete the version.Protection against most accidental or unauthorized changes, with a way for administrators to override.
Compliance modeNobody, including the root user, can overwrite or delete the version, or shorten the retention period, until it ends.Regulatory requirements that demand true immutability.

5.5 S3 Glacier Vault Lock

  • S3 Glacier Vault Lock also uses a write once, read many (WORM) model, but it works through a vault lock policy.
  • You create a Vault Lock policy and then lock it. After that, the policy can no longer be changed or deleted.
  • It helps with compliance and data retention.
  • Object Lock protects object versions in an S3 bucket. Vault Lock protects an S3 Glacier vault with a locked policy.

5.6 Choosing a Protection Feature

RequirementFeature
Recover from an accidental overwrite or delete.Versioning.
Require a second factor for permanent deletes.MFA Delete.
Make data immutable for a fixed time, even for administrators.Object Lock in compliance mode.
Block changes, but allow a trusted administrator to override.Object Lock in governance mode.
Freeze data for an investigation with no end date.Legal hold.
Keep a copy in another Region.Replication (tab 6).

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A regulation requires that financial records cannot be deleted or changed by anyone, including the account administrators, for seven years. Which S3 feature meets the requirement?

  • A. Versioning with MFA Delete.
  • B. S3 Object Lock in governance mode.
  • C. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention period.
  • D. A bucket policy that denies the delete action.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. Compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from overwriting or deleting a locked version until the retention period ends.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectMFA Delete still allows an authorized person with the second factor to delete a version.
BIncorrectGovernance mode lets users with a special permission override the lock.
CCorrectCompliance mode cannot be overridden by anyone during the retention period.
DIncorrectA bucket policy can be changed by an administrator, so it does not guarantee immutability.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • Once you enable versioning you can only suspend it. You cannot go back to unversioned.
  • A simple delete in a versioned bucket adds a delete marker. The data is not removed.
  • Compliance mode cannot be overridden by anyone. Governance mode can be overridden with a special permission.

Memory Hook

Versioning = undo. Delete marker = hidden, not gone. Governance = locked with a key. Compliance = locked for everyone.

Trigger 2: "WORM storage, nobody can delete, even the root user"

Trigger 3: "Lock data for an investigation with no end date"

Trigger 4: "Require MFA to permanently delete a version"

6. Replication

Problem Statement

FlashCart must keep a copy of its customer invoices in a second Region to meet a disaster recovery policy, and it wants a copy of its logs in a separate account in the same Region for security analysis. The auditors ask that new invoices reach the second Region within 15 minutes. The team needs to know how replication works and what it replicates.

6.1 What Replication Does

  • S3 Replication copies objects automatically and asynchronously from a source bucket to one or more destination buckets.
  • Cross-Region Replication (CRR) copies objects to a bucket in a different AWS Region. Use it for disaster recovery, compliance, and lower latency for users in another Region.
  • Same-Region Replication (SRR) copies objects to a bucket in the same Region. Use it to aggregate logs, to keep production and test data in sync, and to keep a copy in another account.
  • The source and destination buckets can belong to different AWS accounts.
  • You can replicate the whole bucket, or only objects that match a prefix or tags.
  • The destination can use a different storage class from the source.

6.2 Requirements

  • Versioning must be enabled on both the source and the destination buckets.
  • S3 needs permission, through an IAM role, to read from the source and write to the destination.
  • If the source bucket uses S3 Object Lock, the destination bucket must also use Object Lock.
  • For CRR, the source and destination Regions must both be enabled for the source bucket owner.

6.3 What Is and Is Not Replicated

  • By default, only new objects that you write after you create the replication rule are replicated.
  • To replicate objects that already exist, use S3 Batch Replication, an on-demand job. It also replicates objects that failed replication.
  • Delete markers are not replicated by default, and you can turn delete marker replication on in the rule.
  • Deleting a specific version in the source bucket does not delete it in the destination. This protects the copy against malicious deletes.
  • Replication is not chained. If bucket 1 replicates into bucket 2, and bucket 2 replicates into bucket 3, objects created in bucket 1 are not replicated to bucket 3.
  • Replication is not a backup by itself. If you turn on delete marker replication, a delete can reach the destination.

6.4 S3 Replication Time Control

  • Replication usually takes seconds to minutes, but it has no time guarantee by default.
  • S3 Replication Time Control (S3 RTC) replicates 99.99 percent of new objects within 15 minutes of upload and is backed by a service level agreement.
  • RTC also provides metrics and notifications about replication, so you can watch for objects that are delayed.
  • Use RTC when a compliance or business rule needs a predictable replication time.

6.5 Replication Compared With Other Features

FeatureWhat it doesDoes it protect from
VersioningKeeps old versions of an object in one bucket.Accidental overwrite and delete.
ReplicationCopies new objects to another bucket or Region.Loss of a Region, and account-level problems when you use another account.
Object LockPrevents overwrite and delete for a time.Tampering and early deletion.

  • A. Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control, with versioning enabled on both buckets.
  • B. Same-Region Replication with versioning disabled.

7. Security and Access Control

Problem Statement

Years ago a FlashCart engineer made a bucket of customer invoices public by mistake. Since then the security team wants every bucket private unless a reason is documented. A partner account now needs to read one prefix, mobile app users need to upload a photo for a few minutes without AWS credentials, and servers in a private subnet must reach S3 without using the internet. The team must choose the right access control for each need.

7.1 Private by Default

  • Buckets and objects are private by default. Only the account owner and users that an IAM policy allows can reach them.
  • For new buckets, all four S3 Block Public Access settings are turned on by default.
  • For new buckets, access control lists (ACLs) are disabled by default, because S3 Object Ownership is set to Bucket owner enforced.
  • To make a bucket public on purpose, you must turn off Block Public Access and then grant access with a policy.

7.2 S3 Authorization Model

S3 access can be controlled through these groups of controls:

  • Identity-based controls (User-Based)
    • IAM user policies: control what a specific user can do in S3.
    • IAM role policies: control what a role can do in S3, for example the role of an EC2 instance.
    • Permission boundaries: set the maximum permissions that an IAM user or role can have.
    • AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs): set the maximum permissions for the accounts in an organization.
  • Resource-based controls (Resource-Based)
    • Bucket policies: JSON policies attached to a bucket. Use them to grant access to another account, to enforce HTTPS, or to restrict access by IP address, VPC, or VPC endpoint.
    • Access point policies: the policy of each access point, which gives a team or an application its own access to a shared bucket.
    • VPC endpoint policies: control which buckets and actions can be reached through a VPC endpoint.
    • AWS KMS key policies: control who can use the KMS key that encrypts the objects.
  • Legacy object controls
    • Bucket ACLs.
    • Object ACLs.
    • AWS recommends keeping ACLs disabled and using IAM policies, bucket policies, and access point policies for most workloads.

    Once enabled, you can assign permissions such as Read, Write, or Full Control to specific AWS accounts or predefined groups at either the bucket level or object level. These permissions are stored directly with the object or bucket, allowing fine-grained access control without creating IAM or Bucket Policies.

    Because ACLs distribute permissions across individual objects, they can become difficult to manage at scale. For this reason, AWS recommends using IAM Policies or Bucket Policies for most access control requirements.

  • Guardrails and temporary access
    • S3 Block Public Access: an account-level and bucket-level guardrail that prevents public access, even if a policy or ACL allows it.
    • Presigned URL: a time-limited link signed with your credentials, which lets someone without AWS credentials upload or download one object for a short time.
  • Note: an IAM principal can access an S3 object if:
    • The user’s IAM permissions allow it, or the resource policy allows it.
    • And there is no explicit deny.

These four examples show the common ways to grant access: a bucket policy for public access, an IAM policy for a user, an IAM role for an EC2 instance, and a bucket policy for another account.

7.3 IAM Policies and Bucket Policies

  • A request is allowed only if a policy allows it and no policy denies it. An explicit deny always wins.
  • In the same account, an allow in either the IAM policy or the bucket policy is enough.
  • For cross-account access, both sides must allow: the bucket policy of the bucket owner must grant the other account, and the other account must allow its user or role in an IAM policy.
  • Block Public Access can override a policy that would otherwise allow public access.
  • A bucket policy is a JSON document with these elements: the resources (buckets and objects), the effect (Allow or Deny), the actions (the API calls), and the principal (the account or user).
  • Use a bucket policy to grant public access to a bucket, to force objects to be encrypted at upload, and to grant access to another account.
  • An application on an EC2 instance should use an IAM role to reach S3, not stored access keys.
  • A bucket policy is limited to 20 KB.

This bucket policy denies every request that does not use HTTPS:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::flowcart-media",
        "arn:aws:s3:::flowcart-media/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This bucket policy allows anyone to read the objects of a bucket, which is the policy of a public website:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "PublicRead",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::examplebucket/*"]
    }
  ]
}

7.3.1 Bucket Policy: Restricting Access by Source

A bucket policy can:

  • Restrict access from specific VPC.
    • From a specific VPC: aws:SourceVpc
    • Example: this bucket policy denies s3:PutObject requests unless they come from the VPC vpc-1234567890abcdef0 or an AWS service makes them on your behalf. 
      {
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "PutObjectIfNotVPCID",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket3/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "aws:SourceVpc": "vpc-1234567890abcdef0"
        },
        "Bool": {
          "aws:ViaAWSService": "false"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
  • Restrict access from specific VPC endpoint.
    • From a specific VPC endpoint: aws:SourceVpce
    • Example: this bucket policy denies all S3 actions on the bucket unless the request comes through one of the listed VPC endpoints. 
      {
  "Id": "VPCe",
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "VPCe",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET",
        "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:SourceVpc": [
            "vpce-1111111",
            "vpce-2222222"
          ]
        }
      },
      "Principal": "*"
    }
  ]
}
    • Note: the course slide uses the condition key aws:SourceVpc with VPC endpoint IDs. The condition key for VPC endpoint IDs is aws:SourceVpce. Confirm the policy before you release this lesson.
  • Restrict access from VPC source IP ranges.
    • From VPC source IP ranges: aws:VpcSourceIp
    • Example: this bucket policy denies all S3 actions on the bucket unless the request comes from one of the listed VPC source IP addresses. 
      {
  "Id": "VpcSourceIp",
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "VpcSourceIp",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET",
        "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "NotIpAddress": {
          "aws:VpcSourceIp": [
            "10.1.1.1/32",
            "172.1.1.1/32"
          ]
        }
      },
      "Principal": "*"
    }
  ]
}
  • Restrict access from specific external IP.
    • From a specific external IP address: aws:SourceIp
    • Example: this bucket policy denies all S3 actions on the bucket unless the request comes from one of the listed external IP addresses. 
      {
  "Id": "SourceIP",
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "SourceIP",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET",
        "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "NotIpAddress": {
          "aws:SourceIp": [
            "11.11.11.11/32",
            "22.22.22.22/32"
          ]
        }
      },
      "Principal": "*"
    }
  ]
}

7.4 S3 Block Public Access

  • Four settings control public access: block new public ACLs, ignore existing public ACLs, block new public bucket policies, and restrict access to buckets that have public policies.
  • These settings exist to prevent company data leaks. If you know that a bucket should never be public, leave them on.
  • You can apply them to one bucket or to the whole account.
  • An account-level setting applies to all buckets of the account, and it is the strongest guardrail.
  • If a new bucket needs public access, you must turn the settings off first. A policy that grants public access is rejected while the settings are on.

7.5 Object Ownership and ACLs

  • Bucket owner enforced is the default. ACLs are disabled, and the bucket owner owns every object, whoever uploads it.
  • With ACLs disabled, you manage access only with policies. This is the recommended setup.
  • You can enable ACLs by choosing another Object Ownership setting, but most workloads do not need them.
  • Object ACLs give finer-grained control, and bucket ACLs are less common. Both can be disabled.

7.6 Presigned URLs

  • A presigned URL gives temporary access to one object, for either download or upload, without AWS credentials.
  • You create it with your own credentials, and it carries the permissions of the creator.
  • You can generate a presigned URL with the S3 console, the AWS CLI, or an SDK.
  • The URL expires after a time that you choose. In the S3 console, the time is from 1 minute up to 720 minutes (12 hours). With the AWS CLI, you set it in seconds with the --expires-in parameter. The default is 3,600 seconds and the maximum is 604,800 seconds, about 168 hours.
  • Users who receive a presigned URL inherit the permissions of the user that generated it, for GET and PUT requests.
  • Examples: allow only logged-in users to download a premium video, allow an ever-changing list of users to download files with dynamically generated URLs, or let a user upload a file to a precise location in your bucket for a short time.

7.7 S3 Access Points

  • Using a bucket policy to manage access for thousands of applications with different levels of access is complex.
  • An access point is a named endpoint attached to a bucket, with its own access point policy.
  • An access point provides a dedicated endpoint and policy for a specific application or dataset.
  • Use access points to give each application or team its own access to a large shared bucket, instead of one long bucket policy.
  • Each access point has its own DNS name, for an internet origin or a VPC origin, and an access point policy that works like a bucket policy, so that you manage security at scale.
  • Example: a Finance access point grants read and write to the /finance prefix for the finance users, a Sales access point grants read and write to /sales, and an Analytics access point grants read to the entire bucket.
  • An access point can allow requests only from a specific VPC.

7.7.1 S3 Access Points: Example Policy

This policy allows the FinanceTeamRole role to read objects through the finance access point.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AllowFinanceTeamRead",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/FinanceTeamRole"
      },
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:123456789012:accesspoint/finance/object/*"
    }
  ]
}

7.8 Private Network Access With VPC Endpoints

  • A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 lets resources in a VPC reach S3 without an internet gateway or NAT gateway. It adds a route to the route table, and it has no additional charge.
  • An interface VPC endpoint uses AWS PrivateLink. It gives S3 a private IP address in the VPC, and it can be reached from on premises through a VPN or AWS Direct Connect.
  • A bucket policy can allow requests only from a given endpoint or VPC, for example with the aws:sourceVpce condition.

7.9 Access Points With a VPC Origin

  • You can define an access point so that it is reachable only from within a VPC. This is a VPC origin.
  • You must create a VPC endpoint, either a gateway endpoint or an interface endpoint, to reach the access point.
  • The VPC endpoint policy must allow access to the target bucket and to the access point.

7.10 Monitoring and Auditing

  • S3 server access logs record requests to a bucket (tab 11).
  • AWS CloudTrail data events record object-level API calls.
  • IAM Access Analyzer for S3 shows buckets that are public or shared with other accounts.
  • Amazon Macie finds sensitive data, such as personal information, in S3 (tab 12).

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: EC2 instances in a private subnet must read objects from S3. The company does not allow traffic over the internet and wants no extra data processing charges. What should the architect do?

  • A. Create a NAT gateway and route S3 traffic through it.
  • B. Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add it to the route table.
  • C. Assign public IP addresses to the instances.
  • D. Make the bucket public.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: B. A gateway VPC endpoint gives private access to S3 with a route table entry and no additional charge.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA NAT gateway sends traffic through the internet path and adds hourly and data processing charges.
BCorrectA gateway VPC endpoint keeps traffic on the AWS network at no extra charge.
CIncorrectPublic IP addresses use the internet, which the company does not allow.
DIncorrectA public bucket exposes the data to everyone.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • New buckets are private, with Block Public Access on and ACLs off.
  • An explicit deny always wins. Cross-account access needs an allow on both sides.
  • Use a presigned URL for temporary access, and a gateway VPC endpoint for private access from a VPC.

Memory Hook

Private first. Policy to allow. Block Public Access to guard. Presigned for a short link. Endpoint for a private path.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Temporary access to one object without credentials"
→ Presigned URL

Trigger 2: "Private access from a VPC without the internet"
→ Gateway VPC endpoint for S3

Trigger 3: "Prevent anyone from making buckets public"
→ S3 Block Public Access at the account level

Trigger 4: "Grant another AWS account access to a bucket"
→ Bucket policy, plus an IAM policy in the other account

Trigger 5: "Enforce HTTPS for all requests"
→ Bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SecureTransport is false

  • Blog S3 Block Public Access and ACLs disabled for new buckets
  • Docs Sharing objects with presigned URLs

8. Encryption

Problem Statement

FlashCart must show auditors that customer data is encrypted in transit and at rest, that the company can see who used each encryption key, and that one regulated dataset uses keys that the company controls. The team must understand the encryption options in Amazon S3 and pick the right one for each requirement.

8.1 Encryption in Transit

  • Encryption in transit is also called encryption in flight, or SSL and TLS.
  • S3 exposes two endpoints: an HTTP endpoint, which is not encrypted, and an HTTPS endpoint, which encrypts data in flight with Transport Layer Security (TLS).
  • HTTPS is recommended, and it is mandatory for SSE-C. Most clients use the HTTPS endpoint by default.
  • Use a bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SecureTransport is false, to force HTTPS (tab 7).

8.2 Encryption at Rest

  • Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk. S3 offers server-side encryption (SSE), where S3 encrypts the object when it stores it, and client-side encryption, where you encrypt before you upload.
  • Since January 2023, S3 encrypts all new objects with SSE-S3 by default. You cannot turn this base level of encryption off.
  • You can change the default encryption of a bucket to SSE-KMS or DSSE-KMS.

8.3 Server-Side Encryption Options

You can encrypt objects in S3 buckets using one of the following methods:

OptionWho manages the keysKey points
SSE-S3Amazon S3.The default. It uses AES-256. No extra cost and no key management for you.
SSE-KMSAWS KMS. You control the key policy.Gives an audit trail of key use in AWS CloudTrail and lets you control and rotate keys. KMS request charges and quotas apply.
DSSE-KMSAWS KMS.Applies two layers of encryption to meet strict compliance needs.
SSE-CYou. You supply the key with each request.AWS does not store the key. You must use HTTPS and manage the keys yourself.

8.4 Server-Side Encryption in Detail

8.4.1 SSE-S3

  • The keys are handled, managed, and owned by AWS. The object is encrypted on the server side with AES-256.
  • The upload request can set the header x-amz-server-side-encryption to AES256, and S3 applies SSE-S3 by default if you set nothing.
  • It is enabled by default for new buckets and new objects.

8.4.2 SSE-KMS

  • The keys are handled and managed by AWS KMS. KMS gives you control of the key and an audit trail of key use in AWS CloudTrail.
  • The upload request must set the header x-amz-server-side-encryption to aws:kms.
  • You can use an AWS managed key (aws/s3) or a customer managed key that you create and control.
  • Users and applications need permission on the KMS key, for example to generate data keys and to decrypt, as well as permission on the object.
  • For cross-account access to SSE-KMS objects, the key policy must allow the other account.

SSE-KMS limitation: each upload and download calls AWS KMS, so the KMS limits can affect you.

  • When you upload an object, S3 calls the GenerateDataKey KMS API. When you download, S3 calls the Decrypt KMS API.
  • These calls count toward the KMS quota per second, which is 5,500, 10,000, or 30,000 requests per second depending on the Region.
  • You can request a quota increase in the Service Quotas console.
  • S3 Bucket Keys reduce the number of KMS requests, which lowers the cost of SSE-KMS by up to 99 percent.

8.4.3 DSSE-KMS

  • Dual-layer server-side encryption uses keys that AWS KMS handles and manages.
  • S3 encrypts the object twice on the server side: first with the KMS key and then with an S3 managed key.
  • Use it for compliance standards that require multi-layer encryption. It costs more and adds more latency than SSE-KMS.
  • The upload request must set the header x-amz-server-side-encryption to aws:kms:dsse.
  • S3 Bucket Keys are not supported for DSSE-KMS.

8.4.4 SSE-C

  • The customer fully manages the keys outside of AWS. Amazon S3 does not store the key that you provide.
  • You must use HTTPS.
  • You must provide the encryption key in the HTTP headers of every request.

8.5 Client-Side Encryption

  • You encrypt the data in your application before you send it, for example with the AWS Encryption SDK and a KMS key.
  • S3 stores only the encrypted data and never sees the plaintext or the key.
  • Use it when data must be encrypted before it leaves your environment.

8.6 Default Encryption and Bucket Policies

  • SSE-S3 encryption is applied automatically to new objects that you store in a bucket.
  • Optionally, you can force encryption with a bucket policy that refuses any PUT request without the encryption header.
  • Bucket policies are evaluated before the default encryption.

This bucket policy denies uploads that do not use SSE-KMS:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": { "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This bucket policy denies uploads that do not send the encryption header at all:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*",
      "Condition": {
        "Null": { "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "true" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

8.7 Working With Encryption in Practice

  • To apply new encryption to existing objects, copy the objects in place with the new encryption setting. S3 Batch Operations can do this at scale.
  • When you replicate encrypted objects, the replication rule must allow the KMS keys that it uses.
  • Choose the setting for a new bucket in the console, the AWS CLI, or an infrastructure template. The default is SSE-S3.

8.8 Choosing an Encryption Option

RequirementChoose
Encryption with no work and no extra cost.SSE-S3.
An audit trail of key use, and control over key policy and rotation.SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.
Two layers of encryption for compliance.DSSE-KMS.
The company supplies and manages its own keys on each request.SSE-C.
Data encrypted before it leaves the application.Client-side encryption.
Lower the KMS cost of SSE-KMS on a busy bucket.S3 Bucket Keys.

8.9 Hands-On Lab

Hands-On Lab

Lab Overview:

This lab gives you hands-on practice with encrypting an S3 bucket, an EBS volume, and an AMI with AWS KMS.

You can start the following lab:

  • GLAB 271.2.5 — Encrypt S3 Bucket, EBS Volume and AMI Using AWS KMS

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company must be able to audit every use of the encryption key that protects its S3 objects, and it wants to control the key policy and rotate the key. Which option meets the requirement?

  • A. SSE-S3.
  • B. No encryption, with a bucket policy.
  • C. SSE-C.
  • D. SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. SSE-KMS with a customer managed key gives control over the key policy and rotation, and CloudTrail records each key use.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectSSE-S3 keys are managed by S3, so you cannot audit or control them.
BIncorrectA bucket policy does not encrypt data.
CIncorrectWith SSE-C the company must manage the keys, and AWS provides no key audit trail.
DCorrectSSE-KMS with a customer managed key provides control and an audit trail.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • All new objects are encrypted with SSE-S3 by default, and this cannot be turned off.
  • SSE-KMS gives an audit trail and key control, but KMS request quotas and charges apply. S3 Bucket Keys reduce them.
  • With SSE-C, AWS does not store your key. If you lose it, the data cannot be decrypted.

Memory Hook

S3 keys = default. KMS keys = audit and control. Customer keys = you hold them. Client-side = encrypt first.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Audit key usage and control key rotation"
→ SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

Trigger 2: "Reduce the KMS request cost of a busy bucket"
→ S3 Bucket Keys

Trigger 3: "The company must provide its own key with each request"
→ SSE-C

Trigger 4: "Encrypt in the application before upload"
→ Client-side encryption

Trigger 5: "Force encrypted connections"
→ Bucket policy on aws:SecureTransport

9. Performance and Data Transfer

Problem Statement

FlashCart customers in Asia upload large product videos to a bucket in us-east-1, and the uploads are slow. During a sale, a batch job that writes millions of small order files to a single prefix starts to receive 503 Slow Down errors. The team needs ways to speed up uploads and downloads and to spread the request load.

9.1 Request Rates

  • S3 scales automatically to high request rates, with a latency of about 100 to 200 ms.
  • S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT, COPY, POST, and DELETE requests per second, and at least 5,500 GET and HEAD requests per second, for each prefix in a bucket.
  • There is no limit on the number of prefixes. Ten prefixes can support up to 55,000 GET requests per second.
  • S3 scales automatically, but a sudden jump on one prefix can return 503 Slow Down errors while S3 scales. Spread the load across prefixes, and retry with exponential backoff.
  • The rates apply to each prefix, not to each storage class.
  • Example: bucket/folder1/sub1/file has the prefix /folder1/sub1/, and bucket/1/file has the prefix /1/. If you spread reads evenly across four prefixes, you can reach 22,000 GET and HEAD requests per second.

9.2 Parallel Transfers

  • Multipart upload uploads the parts of an object in parallel and retries only the failed parts (tab 2).
  • Byte-range fetches download different byte ranges of an object in parallel, or fetch only the part of the object that you need, such as a file header. They also give better resilience when a part fails.
  • Use the latest AWS SDKs. The AWS Common Runtime and the S3 Transfer Manager split and parallelize large transfers for you.

9.3 S3 Transfer Acceleration

  • Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers over long distances between a client and a bucket.
  • Clients upload to a nearby Amazon CloudFront edge location, and the data then travels to S3 over the AWS network.
  • You enable it on the bucket and use the accelerated endpoint. A bucket name that is used with it must be DNS compliant and must not contain dots.
  • It adds a charge per GB. Use it when the users are far from the bucket Region and the transfers are large.

9.4 Amazon CloudFront for Downloads

  • CloudFront caches objects at edge locations near users. This lowers latency for downloads, reduces requests to S3, and reduces data transfer out of S3.
  • Data transfer from S3 to CloudFront has no charge.
  • Use an origin access control so that users reach the objects only through CloudFront, and keep the bucket private.

9.5 S3 Express One Zone

  • S3 Express One Zone gives single-digit millisecond latency.
  • Place the bucket in the same Availability Zone as the compute that uses it, to cut latency and cross-zone transfer.

9.6 Moving Large Amounts of Data to S3

NeedService
Move large datasets over the network, on a schedule, from on premises.AWS DataSync.
Move very large datasets when the network is too slow.AWS Snow Family devices.
Let partners use SFTP, FTPS, or FTP and store the files in S3.AWS Transfer Family.
Speed up uploads from users around the world.S3 Transfer Acceleration.

9.7 Choosing a Performance Feature

ProblemSolution
Uploads of large files are slow or fail.Multipart upload.
Users far from the Region upload slowly.S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Downloads of the same objects are slow for distant users.Amazon CloudFront in front of S3.
A part of a large object is needed, or downloads need speed.Byte-range fetches in parallel.
503 Slow Down errors on one prefix.Spread requests across prefixes and retry with backoff.
The lowest latency for an analytics or machine learning job.S3 Express One Zone in the same Availability Zone.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: Users around the world upload large files to a bucket in one Region, and the uploads are slow because of the distance. The company wants the simplest change that speeds up the uploads. What should the architect enable?

  • A. S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.
  • B. S3 Cross-Region Replication to every Region.
  • C. S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
  • D. Versioning on the bucket.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through nearby CloudFront edge locations and then over the AWS network to the bucket.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectTransfer Acceleration is designed to speed up long-distance transfers to a bucket.
BIncorrectReplication copies data after it is uploaded. It does not speed up the upload itself.
CIncorrectIntelligent-Tiering changes storage cost, not upload speed.
DIncorrectVersioning keeps old versions. It does not affect upload speed.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • Request rates apply per prefix: at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second.
  • Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over distance. CloudFront speeds downloads with caching.
  • Multipart upload is required above 5 GB.

Memory Hook

Prefixes scale requests. Multipart splits uploads. Acceleration shortens distance. CloudFront caches downloads.

→ S3 Transfer Acceleration

Trigger 2: "Download parts of an object in parallel"
→ Byte-range fetches

Trigger 3: "Increase read request rate beyond 5,500 per second"
→ Use more prefixes

Trigger 4: "Cache static content close to users"
→ Amazon CloudFront
