10. Website, CORS, and Event Notifications

Problem Statement

FlashCart wants to host its marketing site from S3 with HTTPS and a custom domain. The site loads product images from a second bucket, and the browser blocks them. When a customer uploads a product photo, the company wants a thumbnail created automatically, and the team wants the notification to reach a queue, a topic, and a function. The team must pick the S3 features that cover each need.

10.1 Static Website Hosting

  • S3 can host a static website, which has HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images, with no server-side code, and make it available on the internet.
  • You enable static website hosting on the bucket and set an index document and an optional error document.
  • The website URL depends on the Region. It has the form http://bucket-name.s3-website-aws-region.amazonaws.com or http://bucket-name.s3-website.aws-region.amazonaws.com.
  • If you get a 403 Forbidden error, make sure that the bucket policy allows public reads.
  • The website endpoint serves content over HTTP only. To serve the site over HTTPS and with a custom domain, put Amazon CloudFront in front of the bucket.
  • For direct website hosting, the content must be publicly readable. You turn off Block Public Access and add a bucket policy that allows public reads (tab 7). With CloudFront and an origin access control, the bucket can stay private.
  • Use Amazon Route 53 to point a custom domain name to the site.

10.1.1 Direct Website Endpoint

This configuration may require public bucket access and does not provide HTTPS through the native S3 website endpoint.

10.1.2 Recommended Secure Architecture

CloudFront can make content publicly available while the S3 bucket remains private.

10.2 What Is Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)?

  • An origin is the scheme (protocol), the host (domain), and the port. For example, https://www.example.com has the implied port 443 for HTTPS, and 80 for HTTP.
  • CORS is a mechanism of the web browser that allows requests to other origins while a user visits the main origin.
  • Same origin: http://example.com/app1 and http://example.com/app2. Different origins: http://www.example.com and http://other.example.com.
  • The browser does not fulfill a request to another origin unless that origin allows it with CORS headers, such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • For a cross-origin request, the browser first sends a preflight request with the OPTIONS method and the Origin header. The other server answers with headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Methods. If they allow the request, the browser sends it.

10.2.1 CORS on an S3 Bucket

  • If a client makes a cross-origin request to an S3 bucket, you must enable the correct CORS headers on the bucket. This is a popular exam question.
  • You can allow a specific origin or *, which means all origins.
  • Example: a web page in one static website bucket loads images from another static website bucket. The second bucket needs a CORS configuration that allows the website origin of the first bucket.

This CORS configuration lets one site read objects:

[
  {
    "AllowedOrigins": ["https://www.flowcart.example"],
    "AllowedMethods": ["GET"],
    "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
    "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
  }
]

10.3 Event Notifications

  • S3 can send a notification when an event happens in a bucket, for example s3:ObjectCreated, s3:ObjectRemoved, s3:ObjectRestore, or s3:Replication.
  • You can filter by object name, for example only *.jpg files.
  • Use case: generate thumbnails of images that are uploaded to S3.
  • You can create as many S3 events as you want.
  • S3 event notifications typically deliver events in seconds, but sometimes they take a minute or longer.
  • Destinations include Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, and AWS Lambda, or Amazon EventBridge.

10.3.1 IAM Permissions for Event Notifications

  • S3 needs permission to reach each destination. You give it permission with a resource policy on the destination.
  • Use an SNS resource (access) policy for an SNS topic, an SQS resource (access) policy for an SQS queue, and a Lambda resource policy for a Lambda function.

10.3.2 Event Notifications With Amazon EventBridge

  • S3 can send all events to Amazon EventBridge, and rules then route them to over 18 AWS services as destinations.
  • EventBridge adds advanced filtering with JSON rules, based on metadata, object size, name, and more.
  • EventBridge supports multiple destinations, for example AWS Step Functions and Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Data Firehose.
  • EventBridge adds capabilities such as archive, replay of events, and reliable delivery.

10.3.3 S3 Event Notification Exam Scenarios

#ScenarioSolution
1Generate an image thumbnail immediately whenever a user uploads a profile picture into the images/ folder.Use S3 Event Notifications to Lambda. The Lambda function processes the image and creates the thumbnails.
2A compliance team wants to audit every S3 API call, including PUT, DELETE, tagging changes, access point usage, and internal S3 events, and route them to a central audit account.Use Amazon EventBridge to route all the S3 API calls to the centralized audit account.
3A video-processing pipeline needs to queue uploaded videos for background processing using a consumer fleet that scales automatically.Use S3 Event Notifications to Amazon SQS. The video (object) metadata, such as the path, date, and size, is sent to the SQS queue. Downstream applications such as Lambda or ECS tasks process the messages in the queue asynchronously.
4A news app needs to fan out notifications (email, SMS, mobile push) to multiple subscribers as soon as a new article is uploaded.Use S3 Event Notifications to an Amazon SNS topic. The end users or mobile devices subscribe to the topic.
5A finance team wants to trigger monthly billing workflows across multiple AWS accounts whenever a .csv report lands in the reports/ folder.Use Amazon EventBridge to trigger an AWS Step Functions workflow across multiple AWS accounts.
6A media archive system wants to process archived files automatically using Lambda when a Glacier restore completes.Use S3 Event Notifications to Lambda when the Glacier restore event is generated.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company hosts a static website in an S3 bucket. The company needs HTTPS, a custom domain name, and wants to keep the bucket private. What should the architect do?

  • A. Enable static website hosting and use the website endpoint over HTTPS.
  • B. Put Amazon CloudFront in front of the bucket, with an origin access control, and use a custom domain.
  • C. Make the bucket public and use Requester Pays.
  • D. Enable Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: B. The S3 website endpoint supports HTTP only. CloudFront provides HTTPS and a custom domain, and an origin access control keeps the bucket private.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectThe S3 website endpoint does not support HTTPS.
BCorrectCloudFront adds HTTPS and a custom domain, and an origin access control keeps the bucket private.
CIncorrectA public bucket is not private, and Requester Pays does not provide HTTPS.
DIncorrectTransfer Acceleration speeds uploads. It does not add HTTPS to a website.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A web page that is served from one S3 static website bucket loads images from a second S3 bucket, and the browser blocks the image requests. What should the architect configure?

  • A. A bucket policy on the first bucket that allows s3:GetObject.
  • B. S3 Transfer Acceleration on the second bucket.
  • C. A CORS configuration on the second bucket that allows the origin of the first bucket.
  • D. S3 Versioning on both buckets.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. The browser blocks cross-origin requests unless the other origin allows them. A CORS configuration on the bucket that holds the images allows the origin of the page.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectThe block comes from the browser CORS check, not from missing bucket permissions on the first bucket.
BIncorrectTransfer Acceleration affects transfer speed, not browser access rules.
CCorrectThe second bucket must return CORS headers that allow the origin of the first bucket.
DIncorrectVersioning does not change cross-origin behavior.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • The S3 static website endpoint supports HTTP only. Use CloudFront for HTTPS.
  • A browser that blocks a request to another bucket or site needs a CORS configuration on the target bucket. CORS is a popular exam question.
  • Event notifications go to SNS, SQS, Lambda, or EventBridge, and each destination needs a resource policy that allows S3.

Memory Hook

Website = static only. HTTPS = CloudFront. Blocked by the browser = CORS. Event = SNS, SQS, Lambda, EventBridge.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Host a static website with HTTPS and a custom domain"
→ S3 with Amazon CloudFront and Route 53

Trigger 2: "403 Forbidden on an S3 website"
→ Check that the bucket policy allows public reads

Trigger 3: "Browser blocks a request to a bucket from another site"
→ CORS configuration on the target bucket

Trigger 4: "Run code when an object is uploaded"
→ S3 event notification to AWS Lambda

Trigger 5: "Advanced filtering and many targets for S3 events"
→ Amazon EventBridge

11. Management, Monitoring, and Logging

Problem Statement

FlashCart’s security team wants to know who accesses its buckets, including requests that are denied. The auditors ask for a list of all objects with their encryption status, and the team finds thousands of old objects that are not encrypted with the right key. A research partner downloads large datasets, and FlashCart wants the partner to pay for the downloads. The finance team wants to see which buckets grow fastest. The team must pick the S3 tools for logging, bulk work, and visibility.

11.1 S3 Server Access Logs

  • For audit purposes, you can log all access to an S3 bucket.
  • Any request made to S3, from any account, authorized or denied, is logged into another S3 bucket.
  • You can analyze the logs with data analysis tools.
  • The target logging bucket must be in the same Region as the monitored bucket.
  • Server access logs are separate from AWS CloudTrail data events, which record object-level API calls.

Warning: do not set the logging bucket to be the monitored bucket. It creates a logging loop, and the bucket grows exponentially.

11.2 Requester Pays

  • In general, the bucket owner pays for all S3 storage and data transfer costs of the bucket.
  • With a Requester Pays bucket, the requester, not the owner, pays for the request and the data download. The owner still pays for the storage.
  • It helps when you want to share large datasets with other accounts.
  • The requester must be authenticated in AWS. It cannot be anonymous.

11.3 S3 Inventory and S3 Batch Operations

  • S3 Inventory gives a scheduled, flat list of objects and their metadata, such as storage class and encryption status, in CSV, ORC, or Parquet format.
  • You can query and filter an inventory report with Amazon Athena.
  • S3 Batch Operations performs bulk operations on existing S3 objects with a single request.
  • Examples of bulk operations: modify object metadata and properties, copy objects between buckets, encrypt unencrypted objects, modify ACLs and tags, restore objects from S3 Glacier, and invoke a Lambda function on each object.
  • A job consists of a list of objects, the action to perform, and optional parameters.
  • S3 Batch Operations manages retries, tracks progress, sends completion notifications, and generates reports.
  • Typical flow: use S3 Inventory to get the object list, filter it with Athena, and give the filtered list to S3 Batch Operations.

11.3.1 S3 Batch Operations in Detail

  • S3 Batch Operations performs bulk operations on millions or billions of S3 objects in a single managed job.
  • A job operates on a manifest, which is a list of object keys. You can create the manifest in these ways:
    • With an S3 Inventory file or a custom CSV file.
    • By specifying a source and a filter, and letting S3 generate the object list. This is a newer option.
  • S3 Batch Operations supports multiple actions:
    • Copy objects across buckets or within the same bucket. You can also encrypt the objects during the copy.
    • Replace or delete object tags.
    • Modify ACLs.
    • Restore objects from S3 Glacier.
    • Initiate S3 Object Lock retention changes.
    • Run an AWS Lambda function on each object.
  • S3 fully manages the job. It includes retry logic, progress tracking, and detailed status reporting.
  • Use cases: bulk updates or processing, large migrations, metadata cleanup, Object Lock changes, and restoring objects from an archive.

A job follows five steps:

  1. Select the objects: choose the manifest.
  2. Select an operation: choose the action to perform.
  3. Start the job.
  4. Monitor the progress.
  5. Review the output: read the completion report.

11.4 S3 Storage Lens

  • S3 Storage Lens helps you understand, analyze, and optimize storage across your entire AWS Organization.
  • It finds anomalies, identifies cost efficiencies, and applies data protection best practices, with 30 days of usage and activity metrics in the default view.
  • You can aggregate data for the organization, for specific accounts, Regions, buckets, or prefixes.
  • You can use the default dashboard or create your own dashboards, and you can export the metrics daily to an S3 bucket in CSV or Parquet format.
  • The default dashboard shows multi-Region and multi-account data. Amazon S3 preconfigures it. You cannot delete it, but you can disable it.

11.4.1 Storage Lens Metrics

Metric typeWhat it showsExample metrics and use
Summary metricsGeneral insights about your S3 storage.StorageBytes and ObjectCount. Find the fastest-growing or unused buckets and prefixes.
Cost-optimization metricsInsights to manage and optimize storage cost.NonCurrentVersionStorageBytes and IncompleteMultipartUploadStorageBytes. Find buckets with incomplete multipart uploads older than seven days, and objects that could move to a lower-cost class.
Data-protection metricsInsights for data protection features.VersioningEnabledBucketCount, MFADeleteEnabledBucketCount, SSEKMSEnabledBucketCount, and CrossRegionReplicationRuleCount. Find buckets that do not follow best practices.
Access-management metricsInsights for S3 Object Ownership.ObjectOwnershipBucketOwnerEnforcedBucketCount. See which Object Ownership settings your buckets use.
Event metricsInsights for S3 Event Notifications.EventNotificationEnabledBucketCount. See which buckets have event notifications configured.
Performance metricsInsights for S3 Transfer Acceleration.TransferAccelerationEnabledBucketCount. See which buckets use Transfer Acceleration.
Activity metricsHow your storage is requested.AllRequests, GetRequests, PutRequests, ListRequests, and BytesDownloaded.
Detailed status code metricsHTTP status codes.200 OK, 403 Forbidden, and 404 Not Found counts.

11.4.2 Free and Paid Metrics

QuestionFree metricsAdvanced metrics and recommendations
AvailabilityAutomatically available for all customers.Paid, additional metrics and features.
Number of metricsAbout 28 usage metrics.Adds activity, advanced cost optimization, advanced data protection, and status code metrics.
Data retention for queries14 days.15 months.
Other featuresNot included.CloudWatch publishing, and prefix aggregation to collect metrics at the prefix level.

11.5 Other Visibility Tools

ToolWhat it gives you
S3 Storage Class AnalysisRecommendations on when to transition objects (tab 4).
Amazon CloudWatch request metricsMetrics for the requests to a bucket or a prefix.
AWS CloudTrail data eventsA record of object-level API calls.
IAM Access Analyzer for S3Buckets that are public or shared with other accounts.
Amazon MacieDiscovery of sensitive data in S3 (tab 12).
Multi-Region Access PointsOne global endpoint that routes requests to the closest bucket among buckets in several Regions.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company has millions of existing S3 objects that are not encrypted with the required key. The company wants to apply the encryption with the least custom code. What should the architect use?

  • A. A script that downloads and re-uploads each object.
  • B. S3 Replication Time Control.
  • C. S3 Transfer Acceleration.
  • D. S3 Inventory to list the objects and S3 Batch Operations to copy them with the required encryption.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. S3 Batch Operations performs bulk actions, including encrypting unencrypted objects, on a list of objects from S3 Inventory. It manages retries and reports.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA custom script means custom code, retries, and tracking.
BIncorrectRTC affects replication time, not encryption of existing objects.
CIncorrectTransfer Acceleration affects transfer speed, not encryption.
DCorrectInventory lists the objects, and Batch Operations applies the action at scale.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company turns on S3 server access logging for a bucket and chooses the same bucket as the logging target. What happens?

  • A. Nothing. The logs are stored in the same bucket without a problem.
  • B. S3 rejects the configuration.
  • C. A logging loop is created, and the bucket grows exponentially.
  • D. The logs are encrypted with SSE-C.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. Each log object that S3 writes to the bucket is itself a request that is logged, which creates a loop that makes the bucket grow exponentially.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectThe logs would write to the same bucket and generate more logs.
BIncorrectDo not rely on S3 to stop the mistake. Use a separate logging bucket.
CCorrectA logging bucket that monitors itself creates a logging loop.
DIncorrectLogging does not apply SSE-C.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • The logging bucket must be a different bucket in the same Region. Logging into the monitored bucket creates a loop.
  • S3 Batch Operations does bulk actions on an object list, and S3 Inventory provides the list.
  • With Requester Pays, the requester must be authenticated and pays for the request and the download. The owner pays for storage.

Memory Hook

Logs = who asked. Inventory = what exists. Batch Operations = do it to all. Storage Lens = see it all.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Audit every request to a bucket, including denied ones"
→ S3 server access logs to another bucket in the same Region

Trigger 2: "A list of all objects with their encryption status"
→ S3 Inventory

Trigger 3: "Apply an action to millions of existing objects"
→ S3 Batch Operations

Trigger 4: "Share a large dataset and let the downloader pay"
→ Requester Pays

Trigger 5: "Organization-wide usage and cost insights for S3"
→ S3 Storage Lens

12. Amazon Macie

Problem Statement

FlashCart stores customer invoices, support attachments, and exported reports in many Amazon S3 buckets, and several teams upload files every day. Auditors ask where personal information such as names, addresses, and payment card numbers is stored, and the security team worries that a sensitive file may sit in a bucket that is public or shared. Nobody can open millions of objects by hand. The team needs a service that finds sensitive data in S3 and reports it.

12.1 What Amazon Macie Is

  • Amazon Macie is a fully managed data security service for Amazon S3. It discovers and protects sensitive data.
  • Macie can discover personally identifiable information (PII) data, such as names, addresses, and payment card numbers.
  • Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover, monitor, and protect your data in S3. It finds sensitive data, such as personal information, financial data, and credentials, in your S3 objects.
  • Macie triggers an alert when sensitive data is identified.
  • It gives you visibility into the security of your S3 buckets, for example which buckets are public, shared with other accounts, or not encrypted.
  • You turn Macie on, and you do not run servers or write scanning code.
  • Macie works with Amazon S3. It does not scan other storage services such as databases or EBS volumes.

12.2 What Macie Does

  • Inventories your S3 buckets: Macie lists the buckets in your accounts and evaluates their security, such as public access, encryption, and sharing.
  • Discovers sensitive data: Macie scans objects and reports the sensitive data that it finds and where it is.
  • Produces findings: Macie reports two kinds of findings: policy findings about the security of a bucket, for example when Block Public Access is turned off, and sensitive data findings about sensitive data in an object.

12.3 How Macie Finds Sensitive Data

  • Managed data identifiers: detection criteria that Macie provides, which find common kinds of sensitive data such as names, addresses, payment card numbers, and credentials.
  • Custom data identifiers: criteria that you define with a regular expression and optional keywords, to find data that is specific to your company, such as an internal customer number.
  • Sensitive data discovery jobs: scans that you run once, or on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule, for the buckets that you choose.
  • Automated sensitive data discovery: continuous sampling of objects across your S3 buckets, so that you see where sensitive data is likely to be without defining each job.

12.4 Findings and Integrations

  • You can review findings in the Macie console.
  • Macie publishes findings to Amazon EventBridge. An EventBridge rule can start an AWS Lambda function or send an Amazon SNS notification, so the response is automatic.
  • Macie also sends findings to AWS Security Hub, which collects findings from several security services in one place.
  • A finding tells you which bucket and object hold the sensitive data, and what kind of data it is. Macie reports the location and the type of the data. It does not move, encrypt, or delete the object.

12.5 Using Macie Across Accounts

  • Macie works with AWS Organizations. You can name a delegated administrator account that manages Macie for the member accounts.
  • Macie is available in most AWS Regions, and it works Region by Region. You turn it on in each Region where you have S3 buckets that you want to scan.

12.6 Macie and the Other S3 Security Tools

  • Amazon Macie: finds sensitive data in S3 and reports bucket security issues.
  • IAM Access Analyzer for S3: shows buckets that are public or shared with other accounts.
  • S3 Block Public Access: prevents public access to buckets and objects.
  • AWS KMS encryption: protects the data at rest (tab 8).
  • Amazon GuardDuty: detects suspicious activity and possible threats. It does not look for sensitive data in objects.

12.7 Amazon Macie Pricing

Prices change often and differ by Region. Always check the current rates on the Amazon Macie pricing page, and estimate your own cost with the AWS Pricing Calculator.

  • The cost has parts for the evaluation of your S3 buckets, for automated sensitive data discovery, and for the data that sensitive data discovery jobs process.
  • Scanning more objects and more data costs more, so choose which buckets to scan, and schedule jobs for the buckets that matter most.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company stores customer files in many S3 buckets. An auditor asks the company to find all objects that contain personal information, and the security team wants to be notified automatically when Macie finds a sensitive object. Which solution meets the requirements?

  • A. Turn on Amazon Macie, and create an Amazon EventBridge rule for Macie findings that sends an Amazon SNS notification.
  • B. Turn on Amazon GuardDuty and review its findings each week.
  • C. Enable S3 Versioning on every bucket.
  • D. Turn on S3 server access logging and read the logs.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. Macie discovers sensitive data such as personal information in S3 objects, and it publishes findings to EventBridge, where a rule can send an SNS notification.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectMacie finds sensitive data in S3, and EventBridge routes the findings to SNS.
BIncorrectGuardDuty detects suspicious activity and threats. It does not find personal information inside objects.
CIncorrectVersioning keeps old versions of objects. It does not search the content of objects.
DIncorrectServer access logs record requests. They do not show what data the objects contain.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • Macie finds sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not scan databases or EBS volumes, and it does not encrypt, move, or delete the data.
  • GuardDuty detects threats and suspicious activity. Macie finds sensitive data. The two answer different questions.
  • Macie sends findings to EventBridge and Security Hub. Use an EventBridge rule for automatic alerts.

Memory Hook

Macie = sensitive data in S3. GuardDuty = threats. Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub.

→ Macie findings, an EventBridge rule, and Amazon SNS

Trigger 3: "Find sensitive data that matches a company-specific pattern"
→ A Macie custom data identifier

Trigger 4: "Detect suspicious API activity and possible threats"
→ Amazon GuardDuty, not Macie

13. S3 Pricing and Cost Optimization

Problem Statement

FlashCart sees its Amazon S3 bill grow, although the team believes most of the data is old. The bill includes a very large amount of data in S3 Standard, millions of tiny files in an infrequent access class, leftover multipart upload parts, old object versions, and data transfer out to the internet. The finance team asks the engineers to explain what S3 charges for and where they can lower the cost.

13.1 What You Pay For

Prices change often and differ by Region. Always check the current rates on the Amazon S3 pricing page, and estimate your own cost with the AWS Pricing Calculator.

Amazon S3 billing has several parts:

ChargeWhat it billsKey points
StorageThe data you store, per GB-month, by storage class.Colder classes cost less per GB. Every object version and every leftover multipart part bills.
RequestsOperations on objects, per 1,000 requests.PUT, COPY, POST, and LIST requests cost more than GET requests.
Data retrievalData you read from the IA and Glacier classes, per GB.S3 Standard and S3 Intelligent-Tiering have no retrieval fee.
Lifecycle transitionsEach object that a lifecycle rule moves, per 1,000 requests.Moving millions of small objects can add a visible cost.
Intelligent-Tiering monitoringA fee per 1,000 objects that S3 monitors.Objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored and not charged.
Data transfer outData that leaves S3 for the internet or another Region.Data transfer into S3 is free. Transfer to an EC2 instance in the same Region and to CloudFront has no charge.
ReplicationRequests, storage of the copy, and inter-Region data transfer.Replication multiplies the storage cost.
Management featuresS3 Inventory, S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics, Batch Operations, and Transfer Acceleration.Each feature has its own charge.
Minimum chargesEarly deletion, and the minimum billable object size.Applies to the IA and Glacier classes.

13.2 Example Rates

Rates differ by Region and change over time. The following example rates are for the US East (N. Virginia) Region. Use them to learn the pattern only. For current rates, always use the Amazon S3 pricing page.

ItemExample rate
S3 Standard storage$0.023 per GB-month for the first 50 TB, then lower tiers.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage$0.0025 to $0.023 per GB-month, depending on the tier, plus a monitoring and automation fee of $0.0025 per 1,000 objects.
S3 Standard-IA storage$0.0125 per GB-month, plus a retrieval fee per GB.
S3 One Zone-IA storage$0.01 per GB-month, plus a retrieval fee per GB.
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage$0.004 per GB-month, plus a retrieval fee per GB.
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage$0.0036 per GB-month, plus retrieval fees. Bulk retrieval is free.
S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage$0.00099 per GB-month, plus retrieval fees.
S3 Express One Zone storage$0.16 per GB-month.
PUT, COPY, POST, and LIST requests (S3 Standard)$0.005 per 1,000 requests.
GET requests (S3 Standard)$0.0004 per 1,000 requests.

13.3 Worked Examples

These examples use the example rates above and a full month of use.

13.3.1 Example 1: The Same Data in Different Classes

The cost of storing 1,000 GB for one month:

Storage classCalculationMonthly storage cost
S3 Standard1,000 GB × $0.023$23.00
S3 Standard-IA1,000 GB × $0.0125$12.50
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval1,000 GB × $0.004$4.00
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval1,000 GB × $0.0036$3.60
S3 Glacier Deep Archive1,000 GB × $0.00099$0.99

13.3.2 Example 2: Requests

Request typeCalculationCost
1,000,000 PUT requests1,000 × $0.005$5.00
1,000,000 GET requests1,000 × $0.0004$0.40

Writes cost more than reads, so many small writes add up.

13.3.3 Example 3: A Lifecycle Rule on Logs

A bucket holds 10,000 GB of logs that nobody reads after 30 days:

OptionCalculationMonthly storage cost
Stay in S3 Standard10,000 GB × $0.023$230
Move to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days10,000 GB × $0.0125$125
Move to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days10,000 GB × $0.00099$9.90

A lifecycle rule lowers the storage cost. Check the retrieval fees and the minimum storage duration of the colder class before you choose it.

13.3.4 Example 4: The Small Object Trap

A team stores 1,000,000 objects of 10 KB each. The data is about 10 GB. In S3 Standard-IA each object bills as at least 128 KB, so the team pays for about 122 GB, which is roughly 12 times the real size. Keep small objects in S3 Standard, or combine them into larger objects.

13.4 Ways to Lower the Cost

  • Use lifecycle rules to move data to colder classes as it ages and to expire data that you no longer need.
  • Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for data with an unknown access pattern, to avoid retrieval fees and manual tuning.
  • Choose the class that fits the access pattern. Do not keep rarely read data in S3 Standard.
  • Watch the minimums. Avoid moving or deleting objects before the minimum storage duration, and avoid tiny objects in the IA classes.
  • Abort incomplete multipart uploads with a lifecycle rule.
  • Expire noncurrent versions in versioned buckets.
  • Reduce data transfer out. Use Amazon CloudFront, keep clients and data in the same Region, and use a gateway VPC endpoint from a VPC.
  • Use S3 Bucket Keys with SSE-KMS to cut KMS request cost.
  • Review replication. Replicate only the data that needs a second copy, by prefix or tag.
  • Use S3 Storage Lens and Storage Class Analysis to find savings.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company stores 500 TB of logs in S3 Standard. The logs are read often for 30 days, then almost never, and they must be kept for seven years. The company wants to lower the storage cost without manual work. What should the architect do?

  • A. Move the logs to an EBS volume.
  • B. Create a lifecycle rule that moves the logs to colder storage classes as they age.
  • C. Enable versioning on the bucket.
  • D. Enable Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: B. A lifecycle rule moves data to colder, cheaper classes automatically as it ages, and expires it when it is no longer needed.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectEBS storage costs more than S3 for large log archives.
BCorrectA lifecycle rule lowers storage cost automatically.
CIncorrectVersioning keeps more data, and it increases the cost.
DIncorrectTransfer Acceleration affects upload speed and adds a charge.

Exam Trap

Remember these three points:

  • S3 charges for storage, requests, retrievals, and data transfer out, not only for storage.
  • The IA and Glacier classes have minimum durations, minimum object sizes, and retrieval fees.
  • Old versions and incomplete multipart uploads keep billing until you remove them.

Memory Hook

Storage + requests + retrieval + transfer. Age the data down. Clean up what you do not use.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Lower storage cost for data that cools with age"
→ Lifecycle rules to colder classes

Trigger 2: "Lower cost for unpredictable access with no retrieval fees"
→ S3 Intelligent-Tiering

Trigger 3: "Reduce data transfer out cost for popular content"
→ Amazon CloudFront

Trigger 4: "Stop paying for leftover upload parts"
→ Lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads

Trigger 5: "Find where the S3 spend goes"
→ S3 Storage Lens

15Temporary access to one object without credentialsPresigned URL
16Private access to S3 from a VPC with no internetGateway VPC endpoint
17Prevent public buckets in the whole accountS3 Block Public Access at the account level
18Audit encryption key use and control the keySSE-KMS with a customer managed key
19Reduce KMS request cost on a busy bucketS3 Bucket Keys
20Slow uploads from distant usersS3 Transfer Acceleration
21Static website with HTTPS and a custom domainS3 with CloudFront and Route 53
22Run code when an object is uploadedS3 event notification to Lambda
23The downloader pays for the transferRequester Pays
24A list of all objects and their encryption statusS3 Inventory
25Cut the cost of old object versionsNoncurrent version expiration rule
26Browser blocks a cross-origin request to a bucketCORS configuration on the target bucket
27Log all requests to a bucket for auditS3 server access logs to another bucket in the same Region
28Apply an action to millions of existing objectsS3 Batch Operations with an S3 Inventory list
29Organization-wide S3 usage and cost insightsS3 Storage Lens
30Decide when to move objects to a colder classS3 Storage Class Analysis (Standard and Standard-IA only)
31An application on an EC2 instance needs to read S3An IAM role for the instance
32MFA required to permanently delete a versionMFA Delete, which only the root account can enable
33Discover personally identifiable information (PII) in S3Amazon Macie
34Notify the team automatically when sensitive data is found in S3Macie findings, an EventBridge rule, and Amazon SNS
35Detect suspicious activity and possible threats, not sensitive dataAmazon GuardDuty, not Macie

15.7 Lesson Summary

This lesson covered the following points:

  • Amazon S3 stores objects in buckets, found by key, with eleven nines of durability and strong consistency. A single object can reach 50 TB, and objects above 5 GB need multipart upload.
  • Storage classes trade cost against availability and retrieval. Lifecycle rules and S3 Intelligent-Tiering move data to cheaper classes automatically.
  • Versioning, MFA Delete, and Object Lock protect data. Replication copies new objects to another bucket or Region, and it needs versioning.
  • New buckets are private, with Block Public Access on and ACLs off. IAM policies, bucket policies, presigned URLs, access points, and VPC endpoints control access.
  • All new objects are encrypted with SSE-S3 by default. SSE-KMS adds an audit trail and key control, and S3 Bucket Keys lower its cost.
  • Request rates scale per prefix. Multipart upload, byte-range fetches, Transfer Acceleration, and CloudFront improve transfer speed.
  • S3 charges for storage, requests, retrievals, and data transfer out. Lifecycle rules, the right class, and clean-up of old data lower the cost.

Memory Hook

Bucket holds objects. Class sets the price. Lifecycle ages the data. Versioning undoes. Replication copies. Policies guard. Keys encrypt. Prefixes scale.

17. Knowledge Check

Answer each question in your own words before you open the model answer.

Question 1: Compare object, block, and file storage, and say when you choose Amazon S3.

Maps to: Objectives 1 and 3 (Analysis).

Object storage keeps data as objects with metadata and a key in a flat namespace, reached over an HTTP API, and it is written as a whole object. Block storage, such as Amazon EBS, is a drive attached to an instance that supports in-place changes. File storage, such as Amazon EFS, is a shared file system. Choose S3 for durable, virtually unlimited storage of unstructured data such as backups, media, logs, and static content.

Question 2: Explain the durability, availability, and consistency of Amazon S3, and the limits on object and upload size.

Maps to: Objective 2 (Comprehension).

Every storage class is designed for eleven nines of durability, and S3 Standard is designed for 99.99 percent availability across at least three Availability Zones. S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency. A single object can be up to 50 TB, a single PUT request uploads up to 5 GB, and larger objects need multipart upload, which is recommended above 100 MB.

Question 3: Recommend storage classes for a product photo, a quarterly invoice, and a seven-year tax record, and justify each.

Maps to: Objective 4 (Evaluation).

Use S3 Standard for the photo, because it is read every day. Use S3 Standard-IA for the invoice, because it is read rarely but must be available in milliseconds, or Glacier Instant Retrieval if it is read about once a quarter. Use S3 Glacier Deep Archive for the tax record, because it is almost never read, a delay of hours is acceptable, and it has the lowest cost. If the access pattern is unknown, use S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

Question 4: Design a lifecycle rule for logs that are read daily for a month, rarely for two more months, and kept seven years.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Application).

Create a rule on the log prefix that moves the objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days. Add an expiration action after 2,555 days, which is about seven years. Add rules that expire noncurrent versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads. Check the minimum storage durations before choosing the days.

Question 5: A user overwrote and then deleted an important object. Explain how versioning helps, and how Object Lock differs.

Maps to: Objective 6 (Comprehension).

With versioning, the overwrite created a new version and kept the old one, and the delete added a delete marker. Deleting the delete marker restores the latest version, and you can restore an earlier version. Versioning does not stop a determined deletion. Object Lock prevents any overwrite or delete of a locked version for a retention period, and compliance mode cannot be overridden by anyone.

Question 6: Explain how Cross-Region Replication works, what it replicates by default, and how to meet a 15-minute target.

Maps to: Objective 7 (Comprehension).

CRR copies new objects asynchronously to a bucket in another Region. It needs versioning on both buckets and an IAM role. By default it replicates only objects written after the rule exists, so use Batch Replication for existing objects. Delete markers are not replicated by default. To meet a 15-minute target, enable S3 Replication Time Control, which replicates 99.99 percent of new objects within 15 minutes.

Question 7: A partner account needs to read one prefix of a bucket, and mobile users need to upload a photo for a few minutes. Recommend the access controls.

Maps to: Objective 8 (Application).

For the partner, add a bucket policy that grants the partner account read access to the prefix, and have the partner allow its users in an IAM policy, because cross-account access needs both. Keep Block Public Access on. For the mobile users, generate presigned upload URLs that expire after a short time, so the users need no AWS credentials.

Question 8: Compare SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C, and client-side encryption, and say which one provides an audit trail.

Maps to: Objective 8 (Analysis).

SSE-S3 is the default, and S3 manages the keys at no extra cost. SSE-KMS uses AWS KMS keys, and it gives control of the key policy and rotation and a CloudTrail audit trail of key use, with KMS request charges that S3 Bucket Keys reduce. SSE-C needs you to supply the key on every request, and AWS does not store it. In client-side encryption you encrypt before upload. SSE-KMS provides the audit trail.

Question 9: Users around the world upload large files slowly, and a batch job receives 503 Slow Down errors on one prefix. Recommend fixes.

Maps to: Objective 9 (Application).

For the slow uploads, use multipart upload to parallelize the transfer, and enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so that clients upload through nearby edge locations. For the 503 errors, spread the writes across several prefixes, because S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per prefix, and retry with exponential backoff.

Question 10: Explain what Amazon S3 charges for, and recommend five ways to lower the cost.

Maps to: Objective 9 (Evaluation).

S3 charges for storage per GB-month by class, requests, data retrieval from the IA and Glacier classes, lifecycle transitions, data transfer out, replication, and management features. To lower the cost, use lifecycle rules to move data to colder classes, use Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns, abort incomplete multipart uploads, expire old versions, and use CloudFront and VPC endpoints to cut data transfer.

Question 11: Design an S3 architecture for a regulated archive that must be private, encrypted, immutable for seven years, copied to another Region, and cheap.

Maps to: Objective 10 (Synthesis).

Use a bucket with Block Public Access on and ACLs disabled, and a bucket policy that enforces HTTPS. Encrypt with SSE-KMS and a customer managed key for an audit trail. Enable versioning and Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention. Replicate to a second Region with Cross-Region Replication, and Object Lock on the destination. Add a lifecycle rule that moves data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after the active period, and use a gateway VPC endpoint for private access.

Question 12: A web page from one bucket cannot load images from a second bucket. Explain the cause and the fix.

Maps to: Objective 9 (Application).

The browser blocks cross-origin requests unless the other origin allows them with CORS headers. Add a CORS configuration to the second bucket that allows the origin of the first bucket, or all origins with an asterisk. A bucket policy alone does not fix the browser check.

Question 13: A team enables server access logs and chooses the monitored bucket as the target. Explain what happens and the correct setup.

Maps to: Objective 8 (Analysis).

Each log object that S3 writes into the monitored bucket is itself a logged request, so a logging loop forms and the bucket grows exponentially. Use a separate logging bucket in the same Region as the monitored bucket.

Question 14: Describe how you encrypt millions of existing objects and how you see S3 usage across an organization.

Maps to: Objective 9 (Application).

Use S3 Inventory to list the objects, filter the list with Athena if needed, and run an S3 Batch Operations job that copies the objects with the required encryption. Use S3 Storage Lens to see usage, cost, and data protection metrics across the organization, accounts, Regions, buckets, and prefixes.

Question 15: Explain what Amazon Macie does, how it finds sensitive data, and how a team gets an automatic alert about a finding.

Maps to: Objective 9 (Application).

Amazon Macie is a data security service that discovers sensitive data, such as personal information, in Amazon S3, and it reports the security of your buckets. It uses managed data identifiers, which are criteria that Macie provides, and custom data identifiers that you define with a regular expression. It scans objects with sensitive data discovery jobs or with automated sensitive data discovery. Macie publishes findings to Amazon EventBridge and AWS Security Hub. An EventBridge rule can start an AWS Lambda function or send an Amazon SNS notification, so the team gets an automatic alert. Macie reports the location and the type of the data, and it does not move, encrypt, or delete the object.
